segments.text: Okay, I think that's most of us. Can everyone hear me alright?
Loud and clear. Morning, everyone.
Yep, you're good.
I can hear you, I just can't find my headphones, so if there's a dog barking in the background, that's Biscuit, and I apologize in advance.
Biscuit is welcome. Biscuit has more tenure than half of this company.
Biscuit has better retention numbers than we do, too.
Ouch. Okay, we'll get to that. Are we waiting on anyone? I see Arjun, Hannah, Sofia. Where's, oh there's Sofia.
Sorry, sorry, I was in the wrong link. The calendar invite had two links on it for some reason.
That's on me, I edited it last night and it duplicated the conference thing. Okay. So, is Priya recording this?
I am. It's recording now, and the notes will go out automatically afterwards, so nobody needs to take minutes. Just talk.
Which is the dream, honestly. Using our own tools, sort of.
Well, not our tool, but a tool. Okay, let's get going, because we have a lot to cover and I want to actually leave this meeting with decisions, not just vibes.
So the goal of this session. It's the Q4 roadmap planning. We have about an hour.
I want us to walk out with three things.
One, an agreed list of what we're doing in Q4, and just as important, what we are not doing.
Two, a named owner and a date for every big item.
And three, some kind of alignment on the AI Insights question, because I know that's been, let's say, a spirited topic on Slack.
Spirited is a very diplomatic word.
I'd say it's been, yeah, it's been lively.
Right. So here's how I want to run it.
We'll start with a quick Q3 retro, just the numbers, no finger pointing.
Then Siobhan's going to walk us through what customers are actually telling us.
Then we'll do the AI Insights debate properly, then platform and reliability with Arjun and Priya, then pricing and packaging with Sofia, then hiring.
And then we'll vote and assign owners.
Are we actually voting? Like, a real vote?
A real vote. Everyone gets three votes. It's not binding, I reserve the right to overrule everybody, but I want to see where the room is.
Benevolent dictatorship. Love it.
That's the startup way. Okay, and one more framing thing before we dive in.
The company goal for Q4 is to get from where we ended Q3, which is about 3.58 million in ARR, to 4.2 million by December 31st.
That's the number I've told the board. And the second goal is net revenue retention back above 110 percent.
Everything we pick today should ladder up to one of those two.
And can I add one, just so we're honest about it?
I think there's an implicit third goal, which is we need a story for the market.
Every competitor has an AI thing now, and we don't.
I'll take that as an input, not a goal, and we'll argue about it in section four.
That's fair. I'll hold my fire.
For about ten minutes.
For about ten minutes, yes.
Okay. Q3 retro. Priya, do you want to go first on the engineering side, or James on revenue?
I'll go first, because mine's shorter and the news is mostly good.
Go for it.
So, Q3 in one line. We closed 41 new logos, which is our best quarter ever, up from 29 in Q2.
New ARR booked was about 612 thousand. The bad part is that most of that is Starter and low-end Growth.
Average deal size actually dropped, from about 18 thousand to just under 15.
And why did it drop? Is that the self-serve funnel doing more of the work, or are we discounting?
Bit of both. Self-serve is doing more, which is good.
But honestly, we did discount more than I'd like on Growth deals at the end of the quarter.
The last two weeks of September were, uh, a little bit of a bazaar.
I noticed. I got three accounts in onboarding with 30 percent off and no annual commitment.
Yeah, those were my calls, I own that. The logic was, get them in, prove the value, expand them later.
Which only works if they stick around. Okay, keep going.
Enterprise. We closed two Enterprise deals, Harbor Freight Systems and Lumen Health, together about 190 thousand.
Pipeline for Q4 Enterprise is 1.9 million, weighted it's probably around 560.
Win rate was 23 percent overall, and that's down from 27.
And where are we losing?
I'll get to that, it's in Siobhan's section too, but the short version is we lost six deals in Q3 where the stated reason was some version of, the other guys have AI.
Six.
Six that I'm confident about. Might be more where they just didn't tell us.
See, this is what I've been saying.
Tom.
I'm holding my fire. I'm just noting it.
Noted. Priya?
Okay. So engineering Q3. The honest summary is we shipped a lot, but we shipped late, and reliability was not good enough.
What shipped. Alerts version two went out in July, and adoption is great, about 44 percent of active workspaces have at least one alert configured now.
The Snowflake connector went GA in August. And we did the new onboarding flow, which Sofia can speak to, but I think it moved trial activation a bit.
It did. Activation, meaning a workspace sends events and builds a first dashboard within seven days, went from 31 to 38 percent.
That's a big jump.
It is. Trial to paid didn't move as much though. We're at 11.2 percent, target was 14.
And then what didn't ship. SSO and SCIM slipped. We said August, it's still not done.
The dashboard builder rework slipped about five weeks, and we ended up descoping half of it.
The SSO one hurts, just so everyone knows. That's come up in every single Enterprise security review.
I know. I know. I'll talk about why when we get to platform, but the short version is that the same three people who own auth also got pulled into every incident.
Which brings us to incidents.
Right. We had three sev ones in Q3.
The worst was August 14th, the ingestion lag, where events were delayed up to six hours for about a third of customers.
Uptime for the quarter was 99.82 percent, and our contractual SLA for Enterprise is 99.9.
So we breached.
We breached for the quarter, yes. Technically we owe service credits to the two Enterprise customers who asked, and we've paid them.
It was about 4 thousand dollars total. The money isn't the problem, the trust is.
And just to add some color on that. The August 14th thing wasn't a one-off.
It's the same root cause as the June incident.
The ingestion workers are sharing a single Postgres queue table, and when one big customer backfills, everybody else waits.
We've known about that for a while though, right?
We've known since March. It's been on the list. It keeps losing to features.
Fair.
Okay, and I want to be clear, that's on me as much as anyone, because I've been the one pushing features.
Let's keep going. Siobhan, retention numbers?
Sure. So net revenue retention for Q3 came in at 104 percent. It was 111 in Q2.
Gross logo churn on Starter is running about 2.9 percent a month, which is high but kind of expected for that tier.
Growth tier churn is 1.4 percent a month, and that's the one that worries me, because those are real companies paying us six grand a year.
Is that mostly the discounted ones?
Some of them, but no, not mostly. Most of the Growth churn is accounts that have been with us for more than a year.
They grew, their event volume grew, dashboards got slow, and they left for something that felt faster or smarter.
So it's performance.
It's performance and it's the, what do I do with this data problem. I'll get into it.
Perfect segue. Anything else on the retro before we move on? Hannah, anything from the ML side for Q3?
Um, just that the anomaly detection model for alerts is live on about 900 workspaces. Nothing else really.
That's great, and that's actually relevant for later. Okay. Siobhan, you're up.
Okay. So for this, my team went through every support ticket from Q3, that's 212 tickets that weren't just password resets, plus the notes from 38 customer interviews, plus the churn exit surveys.
And we tagged all of it. I'll share the doc after, but I want to give you the top four themes, roughly in order.
Great, go.
Theme one, and it's the biggest by a lot.
Customers can see that a number moved, but they can't figure out why.
That came up in 71 tickets and in 24 of the 38 interviews.
The quote I keep coming back to is from the head of growth at Parcelly.
She said, and I'm reading it, your dashboards are great at telling me something is on fire, and useless at telling me where the fire is.
That's a great quote. Can we put that on the wall?
You can put it on the wall. It's a bit painful for a product called Pulse, though.
That's exactly the problem AI Insights solves.
Tom.
Sorry. Holding. Still holding.
I mean, he's not wrong, but let me get through them. Theme two is speed.
Dashboards on large workspaces are slow. We have eleven accounts where the median dashboard load is over eight seconds.
Globex is one of them, and I'll come back to Globex, because it's a big deal.
Is that eleven accounts from the ticket tags or from the telemetry?
Telemetry. Arjun's team gave me the numbers.
Yeah, that's from the query logs. p95 across all workspaces is about 4.1 seconds, which is not great, but for the top fifty workspaces by event volume, p95 is 8.4 seconds.
And a few of them time out entirely on thirty-day ranges.
I've seen demos go sideways because of that.
We use the demo workspace, which is small, and then they load their own data in the trial and it crawls.
Theme three is security and admin. SSO, SCIM, audit logs, role-based permissions.
It's lower volume, only 19 tickets, but it's almost all from our biggest accounts, and it's blocking expansions.
And new deals. I have two Enterprise deals in the pipe right now, Meridian Freight and Castellan, where the security questionnaire literally has SSO as a hard requirement.
What's the combined value of those two?
About 240 thousand a year combined.
Okay.
And then theme four is pricing confusion, specifically the event overages.
People don't understand what an event is, they don't understand why their bill went up, and they find out after the fact.
We had 27 tickets that were basically, why is my invoice higher than I expected.
And three of the Growth churns in Q3 explicitly mentioned a surprise overage bill.
That one's mine, and I have a proposal for it later.
Great. So, those are the four. Now, Globex. Globex renews on January 31st.
They're at 186 thousand a year, they're our second biggest customer.
I had their QBR last week with Greg Holloway and Maya Lindqvist, and I'll be blunt, they are at risk.
How at risk?
I'd put it at maybe fifty-fifty right now.
Greg said, pretty directly, that his team is evaluating Amplitude, and that the two things that would keep them are dashboard performance and SSO.
He also said, and this is interesting, that if we had something that could explain metric changes automatically, they'd pay more for it, not less.
Did he say that? He said they'd pay more?
He said, and again I'm paraphrasing a little, if you could tell my exec team why the numbers moved before they ask me, I would find budget for that.
Okay, I need everyone to remember that sentence.
I also need everyone to remember the first half, which is fix the performance and ship SSO.
Both halves are true. That's kind of my whole point. The AI stuff is a reason to expand.
Performance and SSO are the reason they stay at all.
That's a really useful framing. Hannah, you've been quiet. Does the explain-the-change thing match what you've seen?
Yeah. Yes, it does.
Okay. James, the six lost deals?
Right. So, six deals, about 310 thousand in total ACV.
Four went to Amplitude, one went to Mixpanel, one went to, I think, building it in-house on dbt and Hex.
In five of the six, the AI features came up in the final stage.
Not necessarily because they'd use them, honestly. In a couple of cases I think it was more that the buyer needed something to show their boss.
But that still matters. That's the story for the market point.
It does matter. I'm not arguing it doesn't.
I'm just saying, in two of those deals, if we'd had SSO we might have won anyway, because the AI thing was a tiebreaker, not the main reason.
Can I add one more thing from the interviews? It's small but I think it's important.
Please.
When we asked people what they'd want from AI, nobody said a chatbot. Not one person.
What they said was, tell me what changed, tell me why, and tell me who to ask about it.
It's very specific. It's basically root cause analysis.
Which is exactly the scope of the Explain This Change prototype.
Okay. I think that's a natural place to move into the AI Insights discussion.
Siobhan, thank you, that was really clear. Please send the doc around.
Will do. I'll send it right after this.
So. AI Insights. Tom, you've been holding your fire for twenty minutes. The floor is yours.
And then Priya, I want you to respond, and then everybody else.
Thank you. Okay. I'll try to be concise.
That'll be a first.
Wow. Okay. Fair. So here's the pitch. We build AI Insights as the headline feature for Q4.
The core of it is Explain This Change.

When a metric on a dashboard moves more than some threshold, you click on it, and we tell you which segments drove the change, which events, which properties, and we write a plain-English explanation.
Hannah's prototype already does a version of this.
Phase two, which is not Q4, would be proactive.
We'd push the explanation into Slack or email before anyone asks, which is literally what Greg at Globex said he'd pay for.
And my ask is that we ship a beta to customers by mid November, and that we staff it with, call it, four engineers plus Hannah, for the whole quarter.
Because if we don't have something real by the time budgets get set in January, I think we lose more deals like the six James just described.
Okay. Thank you. Priya?
So, first, I'm not against AI Insights. I want to say that clearly, because I think Slack made it sound like I am.
I think it's the right direction. I think the prototype is really promising.
My problem is sequencing and capacity. We have eleven engineers.

If four of them go to AI Insights for the whole quarter, plus the three on auth for SSO, that leaves four people for everything else, including the ingestion rework that Arjun described, which is the root cause of two sev ones.
And here's the thing that I think gets missed. Explain This Change runs queries. Lots of queries.
It's basically going to slice every metric by every dimension to find the driver.
If our query layer can't load a dashboard in under eight seconds for Globex, it's definitely not going to run a root cause analysis across fifty segments in any reasonable time.
But that's a solvable problem, you can precompute--
You can precompute if you have a working aggregation layer, which we don't yet. That's the ingestion and query work.
Yeah, I want to back that up with numbers, if that's okay.
Please.
So Hannah and I actually ran the prototype against the Globex dataset last week, just to see.
On their thirty-day event table, one Explain This Change run took about 94 seconds and scanned around 1.3 billion rows.
The warehouse cost for that one run was about 60 cents.
Plus the LLM call on top, which is small, maybe four cents.
Ninety-four seconds.
Ninety-four seconds. And if a customer clicks it on every chart on a dashboard, you do the math.
Sixty cents a click. Globex would click that a thousand times a month.
And that's one customer.
Okay, but the competitors are eating that cost. Amplitude isn't charging sixty cents a click.
Do we actually know that? What their thing costs them?
No. But their customers don't pay per click, I know that much.
They also have, what, eight hundred engineers? We have eleven.
Fair. Fair.
Can I say something about the Amplitude thing specifically? Because Greg showed it to me on the QBR.
Please.
He pulled it up on screen share. It's a chat box.
You ask it a question and it builds you a chart.
And he said, and this is a direct quote, it's a nice party trick, but I don't need a new chart, I need someone to tell me why the old chart went down.
Huh.
So I don't think we're behind on the thing customers actually want. I think we're behind on the demo.
Which, to be fair, is what wins deals in the final round.
Sure, but it's not what keeps them for three years.
I have to win them before you can keep them.
And I have to keep them or your new logos just refill a leaky bucket.
Okay, okay. You're both right, and that's exactly why this is hard.
For what it's worth, the chat-box thing is actually much cheaper to build.
It's text-to-SQL on top of our query layer. The expensive part is the root cause search.
So you're saying the thing customers want is the expensive one.
It's always the expensive one.
That's basically the first law of product management.
I thought the first law was, the customer is always right.
The first law is, the customer is always right about the problem and always wrong about the solution.
Okay, I'm stealing that.
Hannah, can the prototype be made cheaper without the rollups? Like, sample the data?
A bit. We could sample ten percent of events for the search, and then confirm the top candidates on the full data.
That might get it to, um, maybe fifteen or twenty seconds on Globex.
But the accuracy drops a little.
How much?
I don't know yet. I'd have to test it.
Okay. That's a useful fallback to keep in our back pocket.
And to be clear, I think that's a good backup plan, but it's not the main plan.
The main plan is the rollups.
Understood.
Okay, but, and I'm genuinely asking, how much of that goes away with the aggregation work?
Like, if Arjun's rework lands, what does that run look like?
Honestly, rough estimate, with pre-aggregated hourly rollups by the top twenty dimensions, it's probably under five seconds and a couple of cents.
But that's the rollup work, and that's six to eight weeks.
So the rollups make AI Insights possible.
The rollups make AI Insights possible, and they make dashboards fast, and they make the ingestion lag problem mostly go away. It's the same project.
That's interesting. So they're not actually in competition. They're a dependency.
That's exactly my point. It's not AI Insights versus reliability. It's reliability, and then AI Insights on top of it.
I hear that. My worry is timing. If the rollups take eight weeks, and they start in October, that's end of November.
Then AI Insights on top of that is January at the earliest. And we've missed the budget cycle.
For what it's worth, the budget cycle point is real.
Most of my Enterprise buyers lock their tooling budgets in December.
Right, but they don't lock them based on a beta.
They lock them based on a demo and a roadmap commitment. You can sell a credible roadmap.
You can't sell an outage.
Well, I've sold a few roadmaps in my time, that's true.
Let's not put that in the recording.
It's already in the recording.
Great. Okay. Hannah, I'm going to put you on the spot, because this is your prototype.
How good is it actually, right now?
Um. So. On our internal eval set, which is about 150 historical metric changes where we know the actual cause, the prototype identifies the right driver in the top three about 62 percent of the time.
Which is pretty good for a prototype.
It's okay. It's not good enough to put in front of Globex.
If it's wrong a third of the time, people stop trusting it, and then they stop trusting the dashboards too.
I think we'd need to be at 75, maybe 80, before a wide beta.
How long to get from 62 to 75?
Maybe six weeks, if I get one more engineer and the rollups.
Without the rollups it's hard to iterate, every eval run takes hours.
Okay. That's really helpful, thank you.
Can I propose something? Because I think there's a middle path here.
Please, yes.
What if we do a scoped beta. Not a launch, a design-partner beta.
Ten customers, Growth and Enterprise only, behind a feature flag.
We pick customers whose data is small enough that it runs fine today, or we precompute for just them.
It gives James something real to demo and something to put in the roadmap deck, and it gives Hannah real feedback to improve the model.
But we don't staff it with four engineers. We staff it with Hannah plus one.
Ten is small.
Ten is small on purpose. We learn, and we don't put our reputation on the line with a 62 percent model.
And I can find ten. I already have a list of maybe fifteen accounts who've asked for exactly this.
Parcelly would be first in line.
And Globex?
Globex, I'm not sure. Their data is huge. If it takes ninety seconds for them, that's worse than nothing.
We could precompute rollups for Globex specifically, as a pilot of the rollup design.
That's actually a nice forcing function for my team. It de-risks the general rollout.
I like that. That's a real test on the hardest dataset.
Okay. I'll be honest, this isn't what I wanted. I wanted a big launch.
But I think I can live with the design-partner version, if, and this is my condition, we commit to a date.
A real date. Not, when the rollups are done.
What date would you want?
Beta live with the first design partners by November 20th.
November 20th with Hannah plus one engineer, and it depends on the Globex rollup pilot being done by, what, Arjun?
If we start Monday, I think the Globex rollups could be ready by November 6th. The general rollout is later.
Then November 20th is aggressive but doable. I'll commit to it if the one engineer is Marcus, because he knows the query layer.
Marcus is great. Done.
Wait, let's not say done yet, Marcus isn't here to be volunteered.
He volunteered on Tuesday. His cost doc is one of the pre-reads for today, actually, and he's been asking to work on this for a month.
It's part of his growth plan.
Okay, great. Then let me say it back so it's crisp, because this is the first real decision of the meeting.
Decision. AI Insights ships in Q4 as a design-partner beta of Explain This Change only.
Ten design partners, Growth and Enterprise tier, behind a feature flag. Staffed by Hannah plus Marcus.
Target: live with the first partners by November 20th.
We do not do a public launch or general availability in Q4.
And the proactive, push-to-Slack piece is explicitly out of scope for this quarter.
Agreed. Reluctantly, but agreed.
Agreed.
Can I still talk about it in sales conversations? Like, as a roadmap item?
Yes, as roadmap. Beta for design partners, GA in the first half of next year.
Don't promise dates to customers beyond that.
Got it. First half of next year. I can work with that.
And, sorry, one thing. We need a quality bar before we turn it on for anyone.
I'd like it to be 75 percent top-three accuracy on the eval set.
Good. Let's make that part of the decision.
No partner sees it until the eval is at 75 percent. Hannah owns that bar.
Okay. Thank you.
And what happens if we're at 70 on November 20th?
Then we're at 70, and we wait.
Fair enough. I'd rather be late than wrong. I think.
That's the first time I've heard you say that.
Don't get used to it.
Okay. Let's move to platform and reliability, because I think a lot of this depends on that. Arjun, Priya, who's driving?
Arjun, go ahead, it's your plan. I'll jump in on staffing.
Sure. So I'll try to keep this tight.
There are three problems, and they all have the same shape.
Ingestion lag, slow dashboards, and our on-call load.
And the root cause is, basically, we built the platform for customers sending ten million events a month, and our top fifty customers now send between 200 million and two billion.
So the plan has three parts. Part one, ingestion.
We move off the shared Postgres queue table onto partitioned Kafka topics, partitioned by workspace.
That means one customer's backfill can't block everyone else.
We've already got Kafka running for the Snowflake connector, so it's not a new technology for us.
Part two, the rollups we talked about. Hourly pre-aggregations for the most common metric and dimension combinations.
Dashboards read from rollups first, and only hit raw events when they need to.
That's what gets p95 dashboard load from 8.4 seconds down to, my target is 2.5 seconds for the top fifty workspaces.
Part three is operational. We fix alerting so the on-call person isn't getting paged for things that don't matter.
Last month the on-call rotation got 143 pages. About 70 percent of those were noise.
Kevin has a plan for that.
A hundred and forty-three pages in a month.
In a month. Kevin had a week where he got paged at 3 AM four nights in a row.
And that's why I'm worried about burnout. Two people on the platform team have mentioned it in one-on-ones.
I don't want to lose people over this.
Understood. That's not acceptable. What's the timeline on all three parts?
Ingestion migration, I'd say the design doc by October 9th, and cutover done by October 30th.
Rollups, general availability for all workspaces by the end of November, with the Globex pilot by November 6th like I said.
And the alerting cleanup, Kevin thinks two weeks, so by October 17th.
And how many people is that?
The whole platform team, so four, plus I'd want one more from product engineering for the first three weeks.
Basically I'm asking for a code yellow.
Sorry, what's a code yellow? Is that a Google thing?
It's a Google thing, yeah. It means reliability is the top priority for a fixed period.
People can get pulled from feature work, and nothing ships that increases risk unless it's critical.
Okay, so a feature freeze.
Not a full freeze. More like, a soft freeze, for a defined window.
I'd propose the first three weeks of October. So October 6th through October 24th. Three full weeks.
Three weeks of soft freeze. Hmm.
Tom, I can see your face.
I'm not saying no. I'm doing math. What's frozen, exactly? Because the sharing work is basically done.
Sharing is fine, Nina's rolling it out this week. That's already in flight, it's low risk.
Okay. And the pricing page changes?
Those are mostly front end and billing config. They land in November anyway.
Then they're fine too. What's frozen is anything that touches ingestion, the query layer, or auth, unless it's part of the reliability work or SSO.
And the dashboard builder v2?
Frozen. Honestly, I think it should move to Q1 anyway, but let's get to that in the vote.
We'll fight about that in the vote.
We will.
What about customer-specific requests? Like if Meridian needs some small thing to close.
Come to me. If it's small and it closes a deal, we'll find a way.
Just don't promise it on the call first.
That's fair. I'll try.
Try harder than last quarter.
Ha. Okay. Noted.
Arjun, what's the risk on the Kafka migration itself? I don't want the cure to cause another sev one.
Good question. The risk is real. The plan is to dual-write for a week.
Old queue and new topics in parallel, and we compare counts.
We only cut over when the counts match for seven straight days.
And rollback?
Rollback is flipping a flag back to the old queue. We'll keep it warm until end of November.
Okay. I like that.
And Kevin's adding a canary for the consumer deploys. That was the main action item from last week's incident review.
Good. Siobhan, from your side, what would a code yellow mean for customers? Do we tell them?
I'd tell the big ones. Not with the phrase code yellow, obviously.
No. Nobody wants to hear their vendor is in code anything.
Right. I'd say something like, we're investing the next month in performance and reliability, here's what you'll see.
For Globex specifically, I think that message could actually help the renewal.
I can give you a one-pager with the before and after numbers. Once we have them.
That would be perfect. Honestly, the funnel improvement Marcus did already helped. Greg mentioned it on the call.
Two point eight seconds to nine hundred milliseconds on their funnels. That was one engineer, one week.
See, that's the kind of thing we should shout about.
I did shout about it. Greg was, and I quote, mildly impressed.
From Greg, that's a standing ovation.
That's basically a parade.
Okay. Then let's capture it. Decision two. We run a reliability code yellow from October 6th to October 24th.
Platform team full time, plus one product engineer.
Feature work that touches ingestion, query, or auth is frozen in that window unless Priya approves it.
And the targets are, Arjun, say them again?
p95 dashboard load under 2.5 seconds for the top fifty workspaces. Ingestion lag under five minutes at p99.
And pages to on-call down by at least 60 percent.
And uptime?
99.9 or better for Q4. That's the SLA, so that's the floor.
I'd also like us to add a public status page.
We don't have one, and customers find out about incidents from Twitter.
Do we really not have a status page?
We have an internal one. The external one has been on the list since, I want to say, February.
Okay. Let's do it. Who owns that?
Kevin can own it. It's maybe two days of work with an off-the-shelf tool.
Great, Kevin by the end of the code yellow then. Priya, you'll tell him he volunteered?
I'll break it to him gently.
Okay. Now SSO and SCIM. Priya, where are we really?
Really? SAML SSO is about 80 percent done. It works with Okta in staging.
Azure AD has an issue with group claims. SCIM is maybe 40 percent. Audit logs haven't started.
What's the date? That's the only thing I need. A date I can put in a security questionnaire.
I'll give you a date, but I want to give you one I'll actually hit this time.
SAML SSO with Okta and Azure AD, generally available on November 2nd. SCIM provisioning on November 16th.
Audit logs slip to Q1.
Can I say November for both?
You can say SSO in early November and SCIM by mid November.
Please don't round it to November 1st, I'll get paged about it.
Ha. Okay. November 2nd and mid November.
That works for Globex too. Their renewal is January 31st, so that gives them two months of having it before they decide.
And the three auth engineers are protected from incidents during that window?
That's the point of the code yellow. Platform takes the incidents. Auth ships.
Okay. Decision three, then. SSO GA November 2nd, SCIM November 16th, audit logs to Q1.
Priya owns it, weekly status in the eng update.
Yep. I'll post it every Friday.
Can I say one thing before we leave platform?
Quickly.
I just want to acknowledge, I think Priya and Arjun were right about sequencing.
I came in wanting AI Insights to be the whole quarter, and I think the rollups argument is correct.
I'd rather say that out loud than just quietly lose the argument.

# Q4 Roadmap Planning — Project Update summary

## Status overview
- Q3 closed at about $3.58M ARR; the Q4 target committed to the board is $4.2M by December 31st, with net revenue retention back above 110%.
- Q3 was a record for new logos (41, up from 29) but average deal size fell from about $18k to just under $15k after heavy end-of-quarter discounting.
- Reliability missed the mark: three sev-1s, 99.82% uptime against a 99.9% Enterprise SLA, and about $4k in service credits paid.
- NRR slipped from 111% to 104%. Growth-tier churn of 1.4% a month is mostly year-plus accounts leaving over slow dashboards.
- Globex ($186k ARR, renews January 31st) is roughly a fifty-fifty renewal risk and is evaluating Amplitude.

## Progress since last update
- Alerts v2 shipped in July. 44% of active workspaces now have at least one alert configured.
- The Snowflake connector went GA in August, and the new onboarding flow lifted 7-day activation from 31% to 38%.
- Trial-to-paid conversion is 11.2% against a 14% target.
- The anomaly detection model for alerts is live on about 900 workspaces.
- Marcus's query planner work cut Globex funnel p95 from 2.8 seconds to 900 milliseconds in one week.

## Risks & blockers
- SSO/SCIM slipped from August because the same three auth engineers kept getting pulled into incidents. It is blocking about $240k of Enterprise pipeline (Meridian Freight, Castellan).
- Ingestion workers share a single Postgres queue table, so one customer's backfill stalls everyone. It was the root cause of both the June and August 14th incidents.
- The top 50 workspaces see 8.4s p95 dashboard loads, and some 30-day queries time out.
- The Explain This Change prototype took 94 seconds and about 60 cents of warehouse cost per run on Globex data. It sits at 62% top-3 accuracy.
- On-call burnout: 143 pages last month, about 70% of them noise. Two platform engineers raised it in 1:1s.
- Six Q3 deals (about $310k ACV) were lost where competitors' AI features came up in the final stage.

## Decisions made
- AI Insights ships as a design-partner beta of Explain This Change: 10 Growth/Enterprise partners, staffed by Hannah and Marcus, live by November 20th if the eval reaches 75%. No GA in Q4.
- Reliability code yellow runs October 6th to 24th: Kafka ingestion, rollups, alert cleanup and a public status page.
- SSO GA on November 2nd, SCIM on November 16th. Audit logs move to Q1.
- New Growth pricing starts November 3rd at $599/month with 20M events included and $25 per extra million. Existing customers are grandfathered for 12 months.
- The staff engineer and CSM reqs are approved now. The ML engineer req opens in January.
- Q4 priorities in order: reliability, SSO/SCIM, AI Insights beta, pricing. Dashboard builder v2 moves to Q1 and the mobile app is cut.

## Next steps
- Priya sends the code yellow staffing plan by end of day tomorrow, and the Olivia Grant offer by next Wednesday.
- Arjun delivers the Kafka design doc by October 9th, cutover by October 30th, and the Globex rollup pilot by November 6th.
- Hannah sends eval updates every two weeks starting October 16th and makes the go/no-go call on November 13th.
- Siobhan signs up 10 design partners by October 24th and holds the Globex call with Greg Holloway by October 10th.
- Sofia delivers the pricing spec by October 15th and drafts the customer email by October 20th.
- Dana delivers the board update by October 9th, and the comp plan fix with James by October 17th.

# Q4 Roadmap Planning — General summary

## Meeting purpose
- Agree the Q4 roadmap: what Northwind is doing and not doing, a named owner and date for every big item, and alignment on AI Insights.
- Every priority should ladder up to $4.2M ARR by year end or NRR back above 110%.

## Topics discussed
- Q3 retro: 41 new logos and $612k new ARR, but smaller deals, a 23% win rate (down from 27%), three sev-1s and an SLA breach.
- Customer themes from 212 tickets and 38 interviews: explaining why metrics moved, dashboard speed, SSO/SCIM, and surprise overage bills.
- AI Insights debate: Tom wanted a mid-November launch with four engineers. Priya argued reliability and the rollups have to come first.
- Customers want root cause analysis, not a chatbot. Greg at Globex called Amplitude's chat box "a nice party trick".
- Platform plan: partitioned Kafka ingestion, hourly rollups targeting 2.5s p95 dashboards, and on-call noise reduction.
- Pricing: the median Growth customer pays about $740/month because of overages. Proposal is $599 with 20M events, plus a usage meter and alerts at 80% and 100%.
- Hiring: budget covers two of three reqs this quarter, and the room chose the staff engineer and the CSM.

## Key takeaways
- Reliability and AI Insights depend on each other rather than competing: the rollups make both fast dashboards and affordable root-cause runs possible.
- The AI features are a reason to expand, while performance and SSO are the reason customers stay at all.
- Tom publicly conceded that Priya and Arjun were right about sequencing.
- The vote confirmed the order: reliability 7, SSO 6, AI Insights 6, pricing 4, dashboard builder 1, mobile app 0.

## Next steps
- Tom presents the doing / not-doing slide at Friday's all-hands and calls the two mobile-app customers.
- James updates the Q4 forecast by October 8th and runs rep training on the new pricing by October 31st.
- Kevin cuts on-call pages by 60% by October 17th and has the public status page live by October 24th.
- Priya shares the notes in the leadership channel.

# Q4 Roadmap Planning — Q&A summary

## Questions & answers
- Why did average deal size drop? Partly self-serve doing more of the work, partly heavy Growth discounting in the last two weeks of September.
- Is Growth churn mostly the discounted accounts? No. It is mostly year-plus accounts whose event volume grew until dashboards got slow.
- How at risk is Globex? About fifty-fifty. They are evaluating Amplitude, and performance and SSO would keep them.
- How good is the Explain This Change prototype? It finds the right driver in the top three 62% of the time. It needs 75 to 80% before a wide beta.
- What does a run cost after the rollups? Probably under five seconds and a couple of cents, compared with 94 seconds and about 60 cents today.
- What if the eval is at 70% on November 20th? Then the beta waits.
- How do we roll back the Kafka migration? Flip a flag back to the old queue, which stays warm until the end of November after a week of dual-writes.
- What date can go in security questionnaires? SSO in early November (GA November 2nd) and SCIM by mid November.
- Does 20M included events hurt margins? No. Infra cost is about $3.10 per million events and heading to about $2, and Growth gross margin stays above 78%.

## Open questions
- Accuracy impact of sampling 10% of events to make Explain This Change cheaper before the rollups land. Hannah needs to test it.
- Whether Globex joins as a design partner. Siobhan will ask Greg on the October 10th call.
- Long-term AI Insights packaging and whether it is included in Enterprise. That will be decided in Q1 once run costs are known.
- Annual discount stays at 20% through Q1. Dana wants to revisit in January.

## Next steps

bullets.text: Why did average deal size drop? Partly self-serve doing more of the work, partly heavy Growth discounting in the last two weeks of September.
Is Growth churn mostly the discounted accounts? No. It is mostly year-plus accounts whose event volume grew until dashboards got slow.
How at risk is Globex? About fifty-fifty. They are evaluating Amplitude, and performance and SSO would keep them.
How good is the Explain This Change prototype? It finds the right driver in the top three 62% of the time. It needs 75 to 80% before a wide beta.
What does a run cost after the rollups? Probably under five seconds and a couple of cents, compared with 94 seconds and about 60 cents today.
What if the eval is at 70% on November 20th? Then the beta waits.
How do we roll back the Kafka migration? Flip a flag back to the old queue, which stays warm until the end of November after a week of dual-writes.
What date can go in security questionnaires? SSO in early November (GA November 2nd) and SCIM by mid November.
Does 20M included events hurt margins? No. Infra cost is about $3.10 per million events and heading to about $2, and Growth gross margin stays above 78%.
Accuracy impact of sampling 10% of events to make Explain This Change cheaper before the rollups land. Hannah needs to test it.
Whether Globex joins as a design partner. Siobhan will ask Greg on the October 10th call.
Long-term AI Insights packaging and whether it is included in Enterprise. That will be decided in Q1 once run costs are known.
